text: The default OS allocator is completely oblivious to NUMA. Unless you intervene, it scatters pages across the socket topology purely based on first-touch, destroying memory locality.
context: On multi-socket systems, Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) means that a core on socket 0 accessing memory physically attached to socket 1 pays a latency penalty of 2–4× compared to local access. The operating system's memory allocator is NUMA-unaware by default; achieving locality requires explicit binding with `numactl` or `mbind`. TLB shootdowns occur when one core modifies a page table entry and must interrupt all other cores to invalidate their local TLB copies, a mechanism that scales poorly as core counts grow. The unresolved tension is that NUMA topology is exposed to the OS but almost never to application programmers, yet ignoring it produces performance cliffs that appear only at scale.

TLB shootdowns occur when one core modifies a page table entry and must interrupt all other cores to invalidate their local TLB copies, a mechanism that scales poorly as core counts grow. The unresolved tension is that NUMA topology is exposed to the OS but almost never to application programmers, yet ignoring it produces performance cliffs that appear only at scale.

text: A typical data race is a logic bug. A NUMA placement issue is a performance bug that manifests exactly like hardware degradation, hidden entirely behind the illusion of uniform memory.
